item.title: The Surprising Worldview of Violent Extremists
item.description:
Politics

The Surprising Worldview of Violent Extremists

How researchers lowered violent extremism among January 6th insurrection supporters.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Worldview is more than religion and politics.
  • Researchers studied 26 simpler and broader “primal world beliefs” (e.g., the world is dangerous).
  • From eco-activists to jihadists, one primal world belief was uniquely related to violence extremism.
  • A new way to target it lowered violent extremism among January 6th insurrection supporters.
Source: Pexels/Engin Akyurt

Co-authored with Dr. Daniel Snook, violent extremism researcher at Florida Gulf Coast University and lead author on the breakthrough study.

When I (Dr. Snook) learned about primal world beliefs (or primals, for short)—people’s basic assumptions about the nature of reality—I immediately began to wonder which might be related to violent extremism, or violence for a religious, political, or social cause.

There are 26 primal world beliefs, such as the belief that the world is safe versus dangerous, interesting versus dull, and beautiful versus ugly (Clifton et al., 2019; Clifton & Yaden, 2021). They have been theorized as lenses through which humans interpret daily life with a potentially massive influence on many of the most-studied outcomes in psychology, such as well-being, depression, and many personality traits. But researchers have not been sure of their role yet.

To really find that out, the field would need a reliable way of changing these beliefs, to determine their effects. Yet no one had studied primals and violent extremism before, so our team was excited to take a first look.

Primals are not specific ideological beliefs such as the White supremacist belief that “White people are the superior race," but views that people have about what is true of the world generally. This makes primals useful for exploring how radicalization occurs in lots of different religious and political ideological contexts.

Our first step was coming up with some hypotheses. If you asked violent extremism researchers like me what primal would likely predict violent extremism, many would probably say the belief that the world is dangerous. Dangerous world belief has a natural link to intergroup aggression (Duckitt et al., 2002). This might go along the lines of, “You threaten or attack us, we threaten or attack back.” So, a person who sees the world as full of threat and danger should be more prone to support intergroup aggression, right?

But what we found instead wasn’t anything we expected.

Lower Meaningful World Belief was related to higher violent extremism.

Meaningful world belief is not the belief that your life has meaning, nor the belief the world has some underlying grand meaning or purpose. It simply concerns how plentiful value or meaning is in the world. Does a typical person, place, thing, or experience we encounter matter or have meaning? Or is that rare, and so things usually don’t matter? If you think most things tend to matter, you’ll have a higher Meaningful score; if you think few things matter, you’ll have a lower score.

In five studies of very different ideological groups—committed Democrats, Republicans, Environmentalists, Black Lives Matter activists, and violent Kazakstani prisoners (a total of 1,518 participants)—we found that, out of all 26 primals, low Meaningful world belief was the top predictor of violent extremism intentions, every time.

The sample of violent Kazakstani prisoners was especially interesting. We compared men imprisoned in Kazakhstan for jihadist terrorism offenses (i.e., terrorists) versus plain old violent offenses (e.g., armed robbery, murder). The terrorists had much lower Meaningful World Belief scores. This means lower Meaningful World Belief predicted something very specific: pre-meditated violence in pursuit of an ideological cause and not just violence in general.

Why did Meaningful World Belief predict violent extremism?

Our interpretation of these results was that maybe if someone believes most things (including people) aren’t likely to matter much, then they may feel it’s justifiable to destroy them to advance one of the few things they believe truly matters: their ideological cause.

To put it differently, it’s probably fine to set off unlabeled fireworks in, say, a desert, be cause there’s very likely little of value out there to be destroyed; just sand. But blowing anything up in, say, an art museum or elementary school? No way: There's lots of priceless stuff there.

How could this finding help in the real world?

Building on this worldview discovery, we designed an intervention to increase Meaningful World Belief, which we hoped would decrease violent extremism intentions. Based on existing well-being practices (e.g., gratitude, mindfulness, and prayer), we wanted to create a way to increase people’s awareness and experience of everyday sources of meaning that they weren’t noticing, and then use that to help re-frame their world.

For the intervention, we asked participants to take three photos on their cellphone of things they thought were meaningful (that had value or mattered) throughout the day, for 9 days in a row. The goal was to keep them looking for meaning all day. At the end of the day, they selected the photo they thought held the most meaning and then wrote a short journal entry on why that photo held meaning.

Each day prompts changed. One day they were asked to look for meaning in their home or neighborhood. Another day they were asked to look for meaning in the natural world (e.g., plants, a sunset, etc.), and so on. The idea was to help people identify often-overlooked meaning in different areas of their lives and thereby help them see meaning more often and in more surprising places.

On day 10, we finally asked them to reflect on what sort of world this is, given so many meaningful things, and invited them to see the world differently.

We then tested this intervention in 430 US Republicans who endorsed the January 6, 2021 capitol insurrection (Study 6).

We found that those who received the intervention had higher levels of Meaningful World Belief and lower levels of violent extremism intentions compared to a control group. Excited, we tested this intervention again among 297 US Democrats and Republicans (Study 7) and found that the intervention again reduced violent extremism intentions compared to an active control group, but this time without changing Meaningful World Belief (an important qualification).

Takeaways

This research is exciting due to three breakthroughs:

  1. The evidence from all seven studies suggests an important discovery for violent extremism research: Low Meaningful World Belief is the primal world belief that best predicts violence for a cause, seemingly whatever that cause may be.
  2. We’ve created a new way of reducing violent extremism that aligns with major motivational theories explaining radicalization (such as 3N Theory; Kruglanski et al., 2019, and Ideological Obsession Theory, Bélanger, 2021).
  3. Finally, this is a major breakthrough for primal world belief research.

While primals have been theorized to influence dozens of major life outcomes, a widespread assumption has been that primals can’t be changed (Clifton & Crum, 2025; Clifton & Meindl, 2022). This intervention tentatively challenges that assumption. Teams around the world are already working on adapting this intervention to change other primal world beliefs to see their impact on different outcomes.

To see the full results of this new research, please see the underlying peer-reviewed study published in Psychology of Violence (Snook et al., 2026).

item.title: Perfectionism in Women
item.description:
Perfectionism

Perfectionism in Women

Women with socially prescribed perfectionism often struggle to like themselves.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • A significant portion of women struggle with maladaptive perfectionism.
  • Some perfectionists believe others need them to be perfect and overly rely on them for self-esteem.
  • Validation is nice but isn't always necessary to appreciate who you are and what you contribute.

Up to 72% of women exhibit perfectionistic traits, with 63% of those traits being considered maladaptive, or largely harmful to one’s well-being (Muscemi et al. 2022). This means that many women are extremely afraid of failing or making mistakes, procrastinate due to immense internal pressure to produce perfect work, and internalize the belief that significant others may demand perfection from them (this is known as socially prescribed perfectionism).

From this, codependent relationships may develop. In treatment, a patient may say, for example, “He stopped telling me I’m beautiful, so I stopped feeling beautiful.” To unpack this: A married woman, who’s devoted both to her husband and her work, chronically struggles to feel competent in either her marriage or her career. She possesses what she believes are objective blueprints for becoming the best wife and employee, again, believing that others expect and demand that of her. She spends an inordinate amount of time both learning her craft and on becoming more attuned to her husband’s desires, including reaching his standard for female beauty.

The Need for External Validation in Socially Prescribed Perfectionism

However, here’s the rub: To fully believe and feel she met those purportedly objective standards for wives and employees, she needs subjective validation—permission to feel good about herself, permission to believe she’s enough. It’s like when a child feels unsure of the quality of their work and asks (and is expected to ask) their parent to check their homework for errors, before asking for permission to play. The socially prescribed perfectionist, even if espousing the virtues of independence and individualism, often carries the deep-seated need for constant approval. Their identity is a mere amalgam of introjects of important others’ perceptions of them, meaning they see themselves only as significant others see them, even if those perceptions are wrong.

Our fictitious patient who no longer feels beautiful may be challenged by her therapist to consider the validity of her belief that her husband doesn’t find her attractive. And she may, in turn, place the burden of proof onto the therapist, not only challenging them to prove to her that she’s wrong about her husband’s perception of her but, even further, to prove to her that she is, indeed, objectively beautiful, worthy of her husband’s praise. Perfectionism searches for more and more proof in an attempt to silence one’s distressing inner chatter. And while the pursuit of evidence is, usually, a good thing, like anything else, it can become excessive. The perfectionist, in reality, needs less proof and to try to make do with what they have.

Questions for Self-Validation and Rethinking Beliefs

Instead, they may consider whether they followed their blueprints. Did you do what you set out to do? Did you produce work that met your goals? And, the most important question in this line of inquiry may be: Can your work be objectively good if a meaningful other fails to acknowledge it? To tailor this question to our patient here, we may ask: Can you still feel beautiful even if your husband doesn’t tell you that you are? Often, our patients become angry after realizing they placed so much emphasis on a man’s opinion of them. Why should anyone else dictate how they get to feel about themselves? Why can’t they feel beautiful or competent because they allowed themselves to?

While keeping in mind that all of us need doses of validation from people we love and admire, we also need to remind ourselves that the truth is the truth, no matter who can or can’t see it. This means that, all being equal, if something is objectively true, we don’t always need someone else to prove to us that it is and if we do, if we can’t see it ourselves (with the evidence at our disposal), chances are that it isn’t true anyway.

Our social system is arguably designed to sustain those in power, but we don’t have to internalize its structure; we don’t have to continue to overly rely on perceived authority figures to tell us how to think about ourselves. So, while we can’t change a social system overnight, we can improve our own thinking and our degree of confidence around it. We can start by questioning social expectations and ask ourselves how many of them we want to meet and why, reconsidering our values. Then, we can consider our contributions and successes, asking ourselves how we can objectively consider them as such. And, if we were to go further, we can even try to embrace our apparent failures. Feminist icon Roxanne Gay remarked, “I embrace the label of bad feminist because I am human. I am messy. I'm not trying to be an example. I am not trying to be perfect.” Implied is the belief that one isn’t loved or lovable for being perfect and one may even infer that one isn’t truly loved if they are. Paradoxically, being a bad feminist is being a good one, because being a good one is to embrace what’s inwardly imperfect, to allow oneself to truly and fully be a human woman.

item.title: Should I Trust My Gut Instinct When Picking a Man?
item.description:
Mating

Should I Trust My Gut Instinct When Picking a Man?

There are times to ignore your gut when dating, and times to go with it.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Our mate preferences evolved to maximize survival and reproduction, not relationship happiness.
  • Our gut instincts are good at picking up on danger and flagging problematic partners.
  • Our gut may not have our best interests at heart when we are attracted to someone.
Source: Kampus/Pexels

Picture the scene: You walk into the bar for your date, and there he is, confident, charismatic, and flashing a gorgeous smile. There's already a glass of champagne waiting for you, and the conversation flows effortlessly from the start.

You're feeling the spark—that intoxicating cocktail of chemistry, excitement, and promise.

And it feels amazing, doesn’t it? I know this; I’ve been there myself many times.

But here’s the thing I want to tell you—and you might not like this—but that spark isn’t necessarily your friend. At least not when it comes to choosing a partner for a happy, lasting relationship. Because while your gut instinct is excellent at picking up on danger and for flagging certain types of problematic men, it’s not always so clever when it comes to getting the hots for a guy and making that the basis for your partnering decisions.

Why Your Gut Isn’t Always Right

Let’s start with a rather illuminating experiment by psychologists Paul Eastwick and Eli Finkel. They asked a group of young speed daters to list what they looked for in a partner. Women typically mentioned ambition and career potential; men noted physical attractiveness. Both genders said personality was extremely important.

But when they actually met their dates face to face? What mattered most for both genders was…physical attraction.

It turns out that what we think we want, i.e., what we know we should be looking for, often flies out the window once we’re in the presence of a living, breathing, gorgeous man.

Now, as an evolutionary biologist, I can tell you this actually makes perfect sense. Our gut reactions evolved to help us survive and reproduce in the Stone Age—the period spanning the vast majority of our evolutionary history. Back then, what a woman often needed in a partner was someone strong, dominant, and genetically fit—someone who could offer protection and healthy offspring.

Fast-forward to the 21st century, and we still have these evolved inclinations—even if we’re well past childbearing age and think we’d prefer someone who’s interesting to talk to and who’ll do his share of the dishes.

So that feeling of “instant chemistry” you get with a man? That fluttering in your belly? Often it’s just your ancient instincts telling you this guy has great genes, a dominant personality, and resource-providing potential.

article continues after advertisement

Unfortunately, the initially compelling traits can often come with some rather unwelcome companions—like narcissism or avoidance.

Or just being a player. After all, a man who excels at first dates has possibly been on a lot of first dates.

The Chemistry Trap

This is why so many of us end up in relationships that start with a bang and end in confusion or heartbreak. Because chemistry, lovely as it is, isn’t an indicator of long-term compatibility.

In fact, men who are naturally extraverted, charismatic, and super-confident are more likely to generate that spark, but they may also be more likely to dominate conversations and show less empathy.

Add to that the “halo effect”—our unconscious tendency to assume that good-looking people are also kind, intelligent, funny, and trustworthy—and it’s a recipe for misjudgment. We end up projecting all sorts of wonderful traits onto someone just because they’re hot. And then we’re surprised when things unravel.

So Should You Ignore Your Gut Completely?

Not always.

Your gut is brilliant when it comes to detecting danger. If you meet a man who seems perfect but something just doesn’t feel quite right, listen to that.

If your stomach tightens when he casually drops a sexist joke, or you feel a flicker of discomfort when his demeanor changes slightly after you disagree with him about something, or somehow things just feel “off”—that’s your subconscious waving a red flag.

article continues after advertisement

Our intuition can be powerful. Research shows we’re especially good at detecting subtle cues of Dark Triad individuals—more on that in this piece where I interviewed Dark Triad expert Minna Lyons of Liverpool John Moores University.

So if your gut says “there’s something not quite right here," it’s probably time to move on.

On the other hand, if your gut says, “this man is dripping sex appeal," then maybe pause before leaping in.

What You Should Be Looking For

Instead of chasing that electric buzz, try looking for a man who makes you feel safe, looked after, and like he’s got your back. The one who actually listens to what you say. The one whose values align with yours, who’s emotionally available, who wants the same things out of life, even if he doesn’t light up the attraction circuits in your brain on day one.

If there’s a bit of warmth, some curiosity, and maybe he makes you smile—that’s enough to get things going and to give him a chance.

Because while the “spark” isn’t a reliable sign of compatibility, its absence doesn’t mean that the relationship is doomed. Desire can grow.

Research shows that when we like someone’s personality—their humour, their kindness, their intelligence—we often come to find them more physically attractive over time.

This is the slow burn, and it tends to produce far more lasting, fulfilling connections than the guys with the fireworks.

The Bottom Line

Trust your gut when it’s warning you of danger, but be cautious when it screams desire—and don’t be too quick to dismiss a good man just because the chemistry didn’t punch you in the face.

We didn’t necessarily evolve to pick a man “naturally” who can make us happy, but we can learn to choose differently—consciously, intentionally, with eyes wide open. And that’s where the good stuff begins.

item.title: What Is Adulthood?
item.description:
Dreaming

What Is Adulthood?

Must being an adult require relinquishing our youthful dreams and individuality?

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • The puer or puella personality is typically quite creative and soulful.
  • Not all puers or puellas exemplify "failure to launch" syndrome.
  • We need to retain some of our childhood hopes and dreams but also adjust to the demands of adulthood.

As noted in Part 1 of this series of posts, as with almost everything in life, there is both a negative and positive side to the puer or puella. So, what are some of the positive aspects of the puer aeternus and puella aeterna personality type?

Psychotherapy for the Puer and Puella Personality

Because such men and women remain in close touch with their eternal or divine inner child, they have more access to qualities like creativity, playfulness, fantasy, imagination, enjoying the present moment, innocence, spontaneity, youthful energy, etc. Many artists, musicians, actors, writers, filmmakers, etc. are so-called puers or puellas. Some others are reformed puers or puellas, having addressed this syndrome in psychotherapy or Jungian analysis in particular.

Becoming an adult for these individuals never meant giving up on their fondest fantasies, wishes, and desires from childhood. Nor should it mean that for any of us. Yes, Freud's "reality principle" requires that we relinquish some of our more grandiose and narcissistic fantasies and tendencies as we transition from adolescence and embrace adulthood so as to adapt to the social structure, limitations, and restrictions the reality of adult life forces upon us. And our childhood wishes may have to be pared down to reality. But this is a far cry from leaving all our dreams and fantasies of fame, fortune, success, love, creativity, beauty, power, etc. behind us, because we still need them. In fact, this can be a big problem for the adolescent approaching adulthood; for if they believe this is what adulthood demands of them, they may angrily rebel, either inwardly or outwardly, against society, becoming cynical, depressed, withdrawn, sullen, and refusing to become part of it. The greatest challenge of adulthood is retaining a close connection with the source of our aspirations, our "inner child," self, soul, or daimon (see Diamond, 1996; Hillman, 1996) while at the same time accepting and navigating the realities, limitations, demands, and disillusionments of adulthood, without becoming too disenchanted, resentful, discouraged, and embittered with life.

The Work Cure

Jung's solution to the pervasive problem of the puer or puella was for them to work. Choosing or forcing themselves to do tedious, difficult tasks of any type to anchor them in reality. This may prove sufficient for teenagers. But is it really a viable antidote for the adult puer or puella personality? Certainly, puers and puellas are particularly prone to procrastination (see my prior post) and tend to disdain and avoid committing themselves to the tedious, mundane, ordinary tasks in everyday life. But simply throwing themselves mindlessly into work, any type of work, while potentially sobering, is not enough. Consciousness is called for: recognizing why they are as they are, its psychological significance, and what makes clinging to their childhood or adolescence so essential to them. This is the purpose of psychotherapy.

Rediscovering and Relating to our Daimon

Most of us as children have dreams, desires, and fantasies regarding what we want to do when we grow up: fireman, astronaut, physician, nurse, auto mechanic, artist, musician, minister, rabbi, parent, president, police officer, psychotherapist, etc. Many of us bury these dreams in adulthood. Jungian analyst James Hillman, in his bestselling book The Soul's Code (1996), sees such childhood fantasies or aspirations as an expression of our daimon, our innate true self or soul. We each enter the world with this congenital inner daimon, which, as Hillman notes, like the acorn, contains the essence of who we truly are and what we are destined to become.

article continues after advertisement

As I write in my own book Anger, Madness, and the Daimonic (1996), "The daimon was that divine, mediating spiritual power that impelled one's actions and determined one's destiny. It was . . . inborn and immortal, embodying all innate talents, tendencies (both positive and negative), and natural abilities. Indeed, one's daimon manifested as a sort of fateful 'soul' which spurred one on toward good or evil." But, for humans, this is never a preordained matter of fate, divine providence, predestination, or predetermination, for as Jung (1968) points out, "the Greek words daimon and daimonion express a determining power which comes upon man from outside, like providence, or fate, though the ethical decision is left to man [my emphasis]."

We are not acorns. Whether one's daimon is expressed constructively or destructively, in good or evil deeds, depends in part upon how the person relates to it, and we are responsible for such crucial choices and their consequences..We can get it wrong. It is when we deny, ignore, or reject this enigmatic daimon (not demon, though this is the source of that negative concept) that we become neurotic, psychotic, or otherwise symptomatic. Like the biblical Jonah, we have refused to faithfully follow the sacred call of our daimon, that innermost guiding spirit or "voice," and, as a result, like Jonah being swallowed by the whale, pay the price.

Dangers of Diagnosing

While the puer or puella personality is not an official psychiatric diagnosis per se, as with any diagnostic label, the problem with employing it as a generic description of someone is that it can become pejorative, judgmental, and prejudicial. And it often carries with it an implicit criticism of such people and their eccentric or non-conformist lifestyles. This is a kind of conscious or unconscious arrogance and grandiosity on the part of the therapist or analyst toward those who deviate from the norm despite the immense pressures society exerts upon them to conform.

There is no "normal," standard paradigm or blueprint, no "owner's manual" when it comes to adulthood and how that should or must look. As with diagnosing and treating psychopathology, the crucial question is always whether the person's way of being in the world is working for them. Or not. Are they fully functioning adults leading satisfying and meaningful lives or frustrated and failing in their efforts to do so? Of course, adults, unlike children or adolescents, by definition are and need to be responsible for themselves, their decisions, and behavior. They are typically physically, neurologically, psychologically, and emotionally more mature and developed than children or adolescents. Adults serve an essential archetypal role and function in society as leaders, teachers, parents, professionals, artists, role models, spiritual guides, mentors, authority figures, protectors, etc. But adulthood, like life itself, is never one-size-fits-all. People are individuals first, and adults second.

article continues after advertisement

Defining Real Adulthood

Here is perhaps the best definition of adulthood I could offer as a psychologist. A real (not merely chronological) adult is someone who accepts rather than denies the existential facts of life; possesses the capacity to give and receive love and to work and support themselves and, when needed, others financially; acknowledges that we are all subject to the influence of the unconscious, complexes, and what Jung called the shadow (see my prior post); knows that we all have a wounded or neglected "inner child" within as well as our daimon (Hillman, 1996; Diamond, 1996) to which we must learn to carefully listen and respond; and recognizes that we are as adults responsible for consciously managing what Rollo May (1969) calls the daimonic, i.e., our primitive passions such as sexuality, the desire for power and control, and particularly, our anger or rage, as constructively or creatively as possible. Last, but not least, real adulthood includes a commitment and quest to find and fulfill our destiny, whatever that may be. To become who we truly and uniquely are and were meant to be. More than this, I could not ask or expect of others or myself.

item.title: Parenting Considerations for Raising Gifted Children and Teenagers
item.description:
Parenting

Parenting Considerations for Raising Gifted Children and Teenagers

Parenting strategies that will benefit your gifted child and the entire family.

Posted August 30, 2026

Source: Pexels/Silverblack/Vitaly Garlev

Some parents, grandparents, and other individuals who participate in raising gifted children as they mature into young adulthood may at first believe that exceptionally talented children and teens will be easy to raise because they are so smart, capable, and effective at certain activities. These teachers and caregivers are not fully informed about working with some types of giftedness and the unique problems that are a part of advanced learners’ approach to schooling.

From my own graduate education, teaching, and social experiences with gifted children and older individuals, including my own, I know that intensity, perfectionism, and social-skills idiosyncrasies create challenges for parents and other caregivers and teachers. These brave and often frustrated educators need help keeping up with gifted learners. Research on educating prodigies suggests that a progressive school that is accelerated and creative is the most likely to help gifted individuals learn to the best of their abilities. A flexible and complex curriculum and teaching approach will hold the interest of their intellectual and creative minds, and a reduction of misbehavior is likely when advanced students are highly engaged in what they are doing.

The Hard Part of Raising Gifted Students

With high intensity and energy, and a strong need to understand some of the difficult ideas that their teachers and parents are presenting, gifted and talented individuals can be challenging in a range of different ways. Their curiosity, emotional concerns, physical energy, and specific interests often tire out teachers and parents. In other words, it is not easy to raise gifted children and work with them as they grow. Patience and fortitude to get them to understand the importance of what you are teaching takes time. Often they do not want to follow the rules or go to school, do their homework, or put away their phone. Questions galore about life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness are never over. There is always a new concern that someone needs to help them process—someone who has perspective and endless curiosity themselves.

The parent, teacher, or adult in charge of the class needs to establish what question or problem comes first, no matter how insistent a high-achieving student is about “managing” (taking control of) what is being taught. For example, space travel is of great interest to all children and teenagers, but especially many gifted learners. When the precocious student is in charge of what they want to learn, chaos can become overwhelming, and learning can become highly dysfunctional. Trying to make current ideas understandable is important but hard to do in a reasonable manner.

The Difficulties Educating Gifted Children and Adolescents

There is no agreed-upon definition of giftedness. The different areas of giftedness make a precise conceptualization impossible in a realistic sense. In other words, being superior in math will look different than being excellent in music or literature. Athletics and music are not really comparable (because of issues of creativity and the uniqueness of sport) to more academic issues that can be more easily cataloged as “giftedness.”

article continues after advertisement

Everyone—parents, teachers, principals, and professors of education—sees giftedness in different ways. This failure to agree on a definition creates the question, “What is the right curriculum and instruction for gifted learners?” My answer is that there is no one curriculum that works for all gifted children.

It is harmful to push or pressure gifted children and teenagers, as it can intensify their perfectionism. Pressure can cause a child to shut down or stop their learning or otherwise burn out their passion.

Further Questions About Educating Gifted Children

  • What is the value of intense acceleration with precocious children?
  • Should gifted children be put together in one class to achieve at a higher level of knowledge or does this limit social and emotional development?

Common Problems for Educators of Gifted Learners to Focus Upon

Intensely bright, creative, and curious learners want answers to their questions right away and in elaborate detail. Pointing out to your passionate child or student that some questions are just too complicated to answer completely and immediately is always helpful and necessary. In fact, it is a very practical educational strategy to teach patience and how learning new things takes time.

article continues after advertisement

I always asked very complicated questions and professors would suggest that my question was for more advanced students. I understand this answer now, after many years of frustration. I was a complicated gifted student, and perhaps the professor wished I would ask fewer questions or be accelerated out of their classroom for another teacher to manage.

Try to learn as much as you can about your gifted son, daughter, or students, always remembering what is unique about how they are exceptional and proficient. Don't let people tell you that a child is not gifted because they don't like to read or do math, etc. Finding special interests such as classical music, art, science, or sports, and developing those interests, is an important step toward figuring out how to challenge a child or teenager. Other parents and family members are invaluable, and you can look to experts for help.

Remember: Gifted children are not advanced in every area of their lives. Often they struggle with schoolwork or socialization. Try to be patient and helpful.

What to Do About Unique Learning Difficulties

  • Treat each student as a unique individual as much as possible. Remember that gifted students are not always high achievers; in fact, they may not like school at all. A talented child might need extra help. A child can be very advanced in one subject, or even just one area of a subject, and not advanced in others. This may bother them because they don’t understand why everything isn’t at the same level of difficulty.
  • Talk to highly talented learners about the ways they are different from average individuals.
  • Challenge your learner when the challenge will be helpful. A student should be ready to learn the material and have an open mind for best results.

Teaching is an art.

item.title: The Dark Side of Parent Support Groups
item.description:
Groupthink

The Dark Side of Parent Support Groups

When echo chambers drown out expertise, misinformation cashes in.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Parent support groups are often echo chambers that spread low-quality information and silence clinicians.
  • Cognitive dissonance and sunk-cost thinking drive hostility toward scientists who challenge misinformation.
  • Costly "coaching" programs fill the gap left by weak evidence and exploit vulnerable families.
Source: AI-Generated

Every day I read through Facebook threads in parent support groups devoted to serious childhood mental health challenges, such as pathological demand avoidance (PDA), disruptive mood dysregulation disorder (DMDD), emotionally based school avoidance (EBSA), and more. These groups exist because parents are exhausted, frightened, and failed by a mental health system that moves too slowly and often lacks the clinical expertise to help their child.

That need is real, but these groups are structured in a way that promotes misinformation, and the harm to children can no longer be overlooked.

A parent posts about a struggle with their child. But much of the advice that follows runs counter to well-established, evidence-based interventions, and some of it can be downright harmful. I reply, politely, citing clinical best practices, but within minutes the harsh responses begin: "You've obviously never met a child with PDA," or "I trust my own gut before your 'so-called' science." A group administrator messages me that I am "upsetting the group members" and a day or two later, I’m removed.

The Echo Chamber

An echo chamber reinforces beliefs through repeated contact with people and information that already agree with them. An analysis of over 100 million posts across multiple social media sites found this same pattern on every platform (Cinelli et al., 2021).

Confirmation bias occurs when we notice information confirming what we already believe and discount what contradicts it (Nickerson, 1998). Layered on top is conformity pressure: In Solomon Asch's famous experiments, participants went along with an obviously wrong group answer on roughly a third of trials (Asch, 1956). That pressure produces conformity bias, where people don't just comply outwardly but actually come to believe the group's position is correct—driven by wanting to fit in and by assuming the group must know something they don't (Deutsch & Gerard, 1955).

What Happens When a Clinician Pushes Back

Another psychological effect that drives these hostile responses is cognitive dissonance. Questioning a so-called "neurodiversity coach" the group already aligns with doesn't just contradict a fact; it implies a parent's past choices might not have been the best and could possibly even be harmful. Holding on to "I did everything right" while also considering "maybe I didn't" results in an unbearable tension. Leon Festinger's classic theory shows the mind resolves that tension fastest by discrediting the messenger, not the belief (Festinger, 1957). Attacking a clinician or scientist is easier than admitting you might have been wrong. The sunk-cost fallacy compounds it: The more time and money a parent has spent on a coach's protocol, the harder it is to admit it isn't working (Arkes & Blumer, 1985). I suspect the sunk cost fallacy is the principal driver of the majority of these hostile responses.

article continues after advertisement

The parents who push back hardest in these groups are often the ones who have built their entire identity around their child's diagnosis (what psychologists call "role engulfment"). They report quitting jobs to devote themselves fully to their child's needs, battling teachers who "refuse to help my child," and fighting a mental health system that "won't listen." Once identity through diagnosis occurs, any mention of an effective treatment isn't just information—it's a threat to the self, triggering the same defensive biases documented whenever a person's sense of self-integrity comes under threat: denial, dismissal, and discrediting the source (Sherman & Cohen, 2006).

Group administrators play a role in the spread of misinformation. Researchers found that admins deleted more comments clashing with their views than matching ones, and were more likely to ban those who posted them (Ashokkumar et al., 2020). Guarding the group's certainty protects an admin's beliefs as much as the group's.

Groups don't just resist correction; discussion among people who agree pushes the group further toward the extreme it favors, known as group polarization (Fraser, Gouge, & Billig, 1971). An analysis of 73 Facebook pages found dissenting content failed to spread, while false confirmatory information spread readily.

Clinicians aren't just ejected from these groups; many self-select out. Research on how people behave in groups found that when a group member's deviation was met with rejection or exclusion by other members, that member became significantly more likely to voluntarily leave the group (Ditrich & Sassenberg, 2016). In doing so, it leaves no one left to challenge the misinformation, leaving the impression that other perspectives don’t even exist.

Why This Matters Even More for Vulnerable Kids

Some of these conditions are based on thin evidence. For example, PDA isn't recognized in the DSM-5 or ICD-11, and a 2026 review concluded current evidence makes it "highly improbable" to support PDA as a distinct diagnostic entity, and flagged potential harms from premature use of the label given the stigmatizing term "pathological" (Company & Rotella, 2026).

Into that gap has stepped a cottage industry of paid coaches whose only credential is having raised a single neurodivergent child. Lived experience is valid and important, of course, but on its own it doesn't qualify a parent to make treatment recommendations. A heart condition in your child doesn't make you a cardiologist.

article continues after advertisement

One program for PDA charges up to $5,000 a month, calling itself "the only program proven to work" while ignoring its own study that found trivial, non-significant improvement in PDA behavior (Carlozzi et al., 2025; At Peace Parents, n.d.). For DMDD, a decades-old off-label medication regimen circulates with claimed success near 90% despite never having a controlled trial (Sunseri, 2025). For EBSA, a structured program combining therapy and parental support returned 96% of adolescents to school within six months (Denis et al., 2026)—evidence that rarely survives a Facebook thread insisting any return to school is traumatic.

Coaches are big business and are unlikely to disappear without community pushback. Utah expanded its authority to investigate unlicensed coaches after one was convicted of child abuse (KSL News, 2025).

What Parents Can Do

You don't have to leave your support group; community and support matter. But skepticism is essential. Notice when a parent or coach dismisses a clinician for lacking lived experience; that's a biased mindset talking. Both lived experience and science are important if we’re going to help kids. If a lone voice raises a question the group doesn't like and the group starts to pile on, that's a big red flag that you’re in an echo chamber. In Asch's experiments, even one ally willing to voice the dissenting view cut conformity errors by roughly three-quarters (Sunstein, 1999). That voice could be yours.

A Call to Action for Group Admins

Moderating is unpaid, thankless work, but leave room for scientific dissent without censoring it. Filtering out cruelty and spam protects your members; filtering out anything that unsettles the group's certainty protects something else.

A Call to Action for Clinicians

If you're a clinician reading this, go into these spaces anyway, even knowing what it will cost you. Speak out: Cite the science, cite the research, say what's true even when it's unwelcome. Prepare to be eviscerated and called every ugly name in the book. Then go back in and do it again.

article continues after advertisement

Somewhere in that thread is a child who has no voice of their own, and a parent who is reading and deciding what to believe. They are the ones being harmed by our silence.

item.title: How to Increase Compassion and Lower Contempt in Relationships
item.description:
Relationships

How to Increase Compassion and Lower Contempt in Relationships

Love without compassion can become possessive, controlling, and dangerous.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • At heart, compassion is appreciation of our basic human frailty.
  • Failure of compassion in love relationships leads to contempt.
  • Despite our prejudice, facts cannot replace compassion or even have much to do with it at all.

At heart, compassion is an appreciation of the basic human frailty we all share. When compassionate, we feel less isolated and more humane. Failure of compassion in love relationships leads to contempt.

Contempt is disdain for the hurt of others. It makes us feel less humane and isolated from loved ones.

Both compassion and contempt are contagious. Around compassionate people, we tend to become more compassionate. Around contempt— even when it’s not directed at us—we’re likely to become more contemptuous.

Both compassion and contempt are subject to projective identification. When we project onto partners that they’re compassionate or contemptuous, they’ll likely become more so. Projective identification is an effective way to bring about change in love relationships, for better and for worse. I urge my clients, and I urge you, to test this hypothesis in your own home. Try a week of projecting onto your partner that they are compassionate.

Compassion Screens

Compassion is a healing emotion and a lifeblood of relationships, but it consumes high mental energy; without compassion screens, we’re easily overwhelmed. Failure of compassion, which feels like betrayal in intimate relationships, often results from compassion screens that are porous or rigid.

With porous compassion screens, we give too much, take on too many burdens, or get fused with others. With rigid compassion screens, we give too little and grow isolated from loved ones. With flexible screens, self-compassion is balanced with compassion for others.

Compassion vs. Facts

Despite our prejudice, facts cannot replace compassion or have much to do with it at all. When my clients cite facts in arguments, they seem mystified that their partners get more upset. When we introduce facts in an argument, the subtext is that our partners have no right to be hurt or, worse, that there’s something wrong with them for being hurt, considering these facts. Hurt feelings are real and deserving of compassion, regardless of the facts involved.

We fight more about disparate interpretations of facts than about the facts themselves, even though interpretations are inherently biased and driven by personal history. In love (and politics), every negative statement is oversimplified, incomplete, subject to interpretation, and, most of the time, hypocritical. When we don’t try to understand our partners' perspectives, we’re likely to consider their interpretations of facts as attempts to mislead, manipulate, or gaslight.

Relationship Repair

Damaged relationships cannot be repaired without unconditional compassion. Look for compassion from offenders, not remorse. Too much remorse leads to more abuse. Remorse keeps abusers in devalued states, where they are more likely to reoffend. It reflects how bad the offender feels, which causes impatience with the repair process: “Get over it, so I can feel better.”

article continues after advertisement

In contrast, compassion is focused on the offended partner’s well-being; it makes offenders want to help in recovery. It puts them in a valuing state in which they like themselves better and are far less likely to abuse again.

item.title: Study Confirms That Political Gender Bias Is Not a U.S. Norm
item.description:
Politics

Study Confirms That Political Gender Bias Is Not a U.S. Norm

Nationwide, more men than women think men make better political leaders.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • U.S. women register to vote and vote more often than men, but remain underrepresented in political office.
  • Biased beliefs appear to impact the gap between voting activity and representation.
  • Gender and political affiliation influence views on whether men make better political leaders than women.
  • Levels of women in office correlate with regional beliefs about men being better political leaders.

Psychologists and demographic statisticians at Tulane University's Newcomb Institute note that women in the United States are underrepresented in elected office compared with their male counterparts, even though women register to vote and vote at higher rates than men. When elected, women achieve more legislatively because they introduce and enact bills more often than male legislators. Female representatives are more likely to build legislation on key areas affecting women and families such as childcare, health care, paid family leave, and sexual harassment in the workplace, and are more likely to support health, reproductive rights, child needs, and prevention programming.

The Newcomb Institute's 2024 study, "Biased Beliefs May Be Impeding U.S. Women’s Progress in Political Leadership," references data showing that women’s representation in elected office is at an all-time high, both in Congress and in state legislatures. However, women remain underrepresented at every level of government. Since 2018, women have made up only 29% of the U.S. House of Representatives and 25% of the Senate. According to the World Economic Forum, the United States lags behind on political gender parity, ranking 63rd worldwide.

48% of the U.S. citizens do not agree that men make better political leaders than women.
Source: Newcomb Institute / Tulane University

The study authors set out to determine what drives the gap between voter activity and representation. Working with the University of Chicago survey research firm, NORC, they asked a World Values Survey question of more than 3,000 adults across the U.S.: How much do they agree or disagree that “On the whole, men make better political leaders than women"?

The Findings

The 2024 results are slightly lower than in 2017. In 2024, only a minority of U.S. adults—12%—agreed that men make better political leaders than women. Many more—48% of U.S. adults—disagreed with the statement, and 40% were neutral.

Globally, based on data from 80 nations, half of the world agrees that men are better political leaders. In high-income nations, fewer people hold this view. For instance, in the Netherlands and New Zealand, only 6% agreed that men make better political leaders, and only 9% in the United Kingdom agreed. Citizens in the U.S. who lean left politically score similarly to the Netherlands and New Zealand.

There's a significant gender split: 59% of women vs. 35% of men disagree that men make better political leaders. better political
Source: Newcomb Institute / Tulane University

Results by Gender

In the United States, men are more likely to agree that men make better political leaders (16%) whereas only 10% of women agree. Of those who disagree that men make better political leaders, 59% are women and 35% are men. Of those who neither agree nor disagree, 49% are men and 31% are women.

Gender and Political Leanings

Among conservative-leaning people, 20% of women and 24% of men agree that men are better political leaders, and 36% of women versus 20% of men disagree. Also, 56% of men report neutrality versus 44% of women.

Among liberals, 6% of men and 5% of women agree with the statement, while 53% of men and 83% of women disagree. Many more men were neutral—41%, compared to 12% of women.

Among moderates, men were more likely than women to agree with the statement (14% of men and 7% of women) or be neutral (49% of men and 35% of women). Women were more likely than men to report disagreement (57% of women and 37% of men).

The researchers also analyzed whether state size and affluence would impact voter opinions. They compared four states: two large states with strong tax bases, California and Texas, and two smaller states with higher poverty levels, Louisiana and Mississippi. Responses to the statement that men are better political leaders correlated with the percentage of women in elected office: California had the most disagreement, while Mississippi had the fewest women in office and the most agreement that men are better political leaders.

The Way Forward

The researchers conclude that the belief that men are better political leaders than women is not normative (i.e., held by the majority) in the U.S., but gender and political divides and state-level differences may impede female representation that matches female registration and voting levels. They suggest that further study of the high level of neutral responses may help develop social and behavioral interventions.

item.title: Does AI Give Workers a Stronger Voice or Just Better Sentences?
item.description:
Career

Does AI Give Workers a Stronger Voice or Just Better Sentences?

AI can help employees write tough messages, but not make them safe to send.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • AI improves writing, but it does not remove the risks of speaking up at work.
  • AI can increase or suppress voice depending on whether employees feel supported or threatened.
  • Heavy AI involvement can make polished messages feel less personal and credible.
  • Employee voice grows when leaders listen, respond, and make speaking up worthwhile.

Right now, someone in your company is writing a message they have been thinking about for months. Maybe they want to question a broken process or challenge a decision from higher-up. In the past, they might have given up halfway, worried that their words sounded either too harsh or too timid.

Now, the employee asks a chatbot to help make the message sound more constructive and sends it just a minute-and-a-half later.

Is this employee voice?

Organizational psychologists define employee voice as speaking up about ideas, concerns, or challenges to improve work, especially when staying silent feels safer. Voice is more about taking a risk than about sounding polished. If the main problem was just finding the right words, AI could help people speak up more. But if people are held back by fear, doubt, or worry about punishment, better sentences alone will not make much difference.

Better writing is not the same as greater voice

The improvement in writing fluency is real. In a study of 453 college-educated professionals, Shakked Noy and Whitney Zhang found that ChatGPT reduced the time required for mid-level writing tasks by 40 percent and improved the quality of the work by 18 percent. It also helped close the performance gap between workers.

This matters in places where polished writing is confused with real skill. Sometimes, a great idea loses out to an average one just because the average idea is written in the style leaders expect. AI can help by making it easier to express complex thoughts, soften harsh wording, or help someone write more confidently in a language that is not their first.

But speaking up is a social act aimed at someone who can ignore, reward, or punish the person speaking. AI can improve the message, but that does not change the power dynamic.

Recent research on AI awareness—employees' recognition that AI is increasingly involved in their work—shows why the outcome depends on context.

Changqing He and colleagues surveyed 203 service employees at two points. Greater AI awareness predicted fewer suggestions for improvement and gave fewer warnings about harmful practices. This drop was partly due to people feeling less confident about speaking up. Job insecurity also played a role. If someone thinks speaking up will not make a difference and worries that technology could replace them, staying silent can feel like the safer choice.

article continues after advertisement

Qingjin Lin and Lyuqi He found the opposite result with 319 hotel employees in four Chinese cities. In their study, employees who were more aware of AI spoke up more, especially if they were eager to learn and had good relationships with their supervisors. This effect was even stronger when employees felt supported by their organization.

These studies show that there is not just one answer. Some employees see AI as a threat that makes them feel exposed, while others see it as a helpful tool they can learn from. The workplace environment shapes which view becomes more common.

Would you rather speak to an algorithm?

A 2026 study adds another perspective. In three experiments conducted in China, Shiqi Wang and colleagues found that people were more willing to speak up to an algorithmic leader than to a human one, but only for tasks involving thinking rather than emotion. When people felt the process was fair, they felt safer and were more willing to share their thoughts.

This does not mean that algorithmic managers are always fair or that people want machines to handle sensitive issues. It shows that who receives the message affects how risky it feels to speak up. Machines might seem less defensive, less political, and less likely to hold a grudge. Sometimes, employees just want someone safe to listen.

The clarity trap

AI assistance can also create a credibility problem. Peter Cardon and Anthony Coman asked 1,100 working professionals to evaluate workplace messages written with different levels of AI assistance. The messages could still appear professional, but medium-to-high AI involvement led respondents to question the sender's authorship, confidence, care, sincerity, and ability.

This study looked at regular management communication, not employee voice, so it is more of a warning than a proven fact. Still, people judge tough messages not just by their content but by what they reveal about the sender. If AI takes away personal judgment, details, and effort, the message might look better, but the sender could seem less trustworthy.

Use AI as an editor, not as a replacement for yourself. Start with your own ideas and evidence. Let AI help with structure or tone, but then add back your own examples and clear requests so the message still sounds like you. If your message could have come from anyone, revise it until it feels personal.

article continues after advertisement

What leaders can do

The most useful evidence shows that listening matters more than technology. In a survey of 500 full-time U.S. employees, Enzhu Dong and colleagues found that when organizations listened to employees during AI training, people felt more independent and capable, had better attitudes about using AI, and made more suggestions. While this study cannot prove cause and effect, it supports a lasting truth: People speak up when they believe someone will respond.

  • Ask about risk, not just access. A polished inbox does not prove that people feel safe. Ask what they considered raising but decided to withhold.
  • Make the response predictable. Acknowledge concerns, explain what will happen next, and close the loop even when a suggestion is not adopted.
  • Separate style from substance. Do not discount a concern because it sounds unusually polished or because an employee used AI to organize it. Examine the evidence and the request.
  • Invite input before decisions harden. During AI rollouts, seek employee concerns while policies and workflows can still change, not after implementation is complete.

The question AI cannot answer

AI is changing how people speak up at work. It can make it faster and less awkward to write tough messages, and sometimes a machine feels like a safer audience. But AI cannot control whether a manager reacts defensively, whether speaking up hurts someone’s career, or whether a warning leads to real change.

The real test of employee voice remains what happens when a tough or uncomfortable message comes in. Do leaders show curiosity? Do they protect the person who spoke up? Do they explain what changed, or why nothing changed?

AI can help employees find better sentences. Only leaders and workplace systems can make those sentences worth sending.

item.title: What Are Dogs Reading in Human Gestures Like the Open Palm?
item.description:
Animal Behavior

What Are Dogs Reading in Human Gestures Like the Open Palm?

A new paper offers valuable advice on studying human-dog interactions.

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • Over-simplification of gestural meanings in human-animal communication can be misleading.
  • Misreading a dog's behavior can have negative effects on their relationships with their own and other humans.
  • Recognizing a dog's emotional needs is, in itself, a pathway toward compassion, empathy, and respect.
An open palm gesture directed toward a dog.
Source: Sindhoor Pangal.

How do dogs understand human gestures? Research cautions us that simple answers to questions like these can be misleading, For this and other reasons I was pleased to read a recent paper by anthrozoologist Sindhoor Pangel titled, "The open palm gesture in human–dog communication: An exploratory synthesis, Human–Animal Interactions." In it, she stresses that perhaps we should move from asking, “Can the dog decode my gesture?” to “What happens to the dog when I make this gesture and how does this impact our relationship?"

The use of an open palm held toward a dog is not novel in our interaction with dogs and is usually understood as a directive: Stop, Wait, or Stay. But her observation is that the same gesture also occurs in casual interactions in which the human does not appear to be asking the dog to do anything.

Marc Bekoff: Why did you write your paper on the open palm gesture?

Sindhoor Pangal: I started noticing the gesture everywhere. In fact, this paper itself carries examples of traffic cops casually using it with street dogs, and the dogs seeming to respond to it as if this were a very natural way for a human and dog to interact.

This fascinated me and I started talking about it with my students. They then began showing me videos of it being used, both with street dogs and with dogs in their homes. Closer examination of these videos revealed something interesting: The effect of this gesture did not seem to be directing them to do anything specific. Instead, I noticed subtle signs of emotional regulations or de-escalation. Then came pilot observations from France and Norway suggesting a possible reduction in pulse in response to the gesture. This got my attention.

So I started looking more closely at the gesture itself. It appears to be an ancient gesture, used extensively by humans across cultures. We use it so frequently that our tendency to use it spills over into casual interactions with animals, as seen in the traffic police examples. Given dogs' remarkable ability to read human body language, it seemed reasonable to ask what repeated exposure to this gesture does to dogs. This paper was born out of that exploration.

MB: How does this paper relate to your background and general areas of interest?

SP: My work straddles two areas: increasing harmony in the human-dog dyad, and the study of free-living dogs in India. The gesture is significant to both.

The more I studied it, the more the gesture seemed to show potential in helping humans and dogs co-regulate emotions in certain situations. A gesture that helps a nervous dog calm down could prevent conflict in an accessible, inexpensive way that requires no training. That’s particularly significant when dealing with free-living animals such as street dogs

With street dogs, I noticed that the gesture was already in circulation among people who interact with them. This raised further questions about gestures in circulation in an informal, largely untrained human-dog environment.

This segues into my anthrozoological work: the co-construction of communication by humans, animals, and society. We communicate reassurance through presence, posture, gaze, proximity, tone of voice, and gesture. Its affect relies on the recipient experiencing this multimodal configuration as reassuring, which in turn is culturally influenced. Communication, thus co-constructed by the recipient, the sender, and society, is where my work is situated.

MB: Who do you hope to reach with this work?

SP: I would like to reach anyone interested in understanding human-dog communication beyond commands and directives. Instead of asking what our gestures mean to dogs, I want us to ask, “What happens to my dog when I use this gesture, in this manner, within this relationship?”

This is particularly significant with free-living dogs. When we approach a dog who has choices about whether to engage with us, communication can be much more about negotiation and social coordination than about obedience.

MB: What are some of the topics you consider and what are some of your major messages?

SP: The main idea is to challenge how we study gestural use in human-animal communication. We typically isolate gestures and look for behavioural responses to them. But gestures are experienced as part of multimodal contextual communication including posture, gaze, movement, voice, proximity, timing, and emotional states. The history between participants also matters.

Gestures like the open palm are not fixed signals with fixed meaning. The open hand is a polysemous gesture whose meaning changes according to how it’s presented, who presents and receives it, and in what context. It’s a co-constructed signal that emerges as a communicative protocol between the actors in a situation. Hence, my paper is an invitation to explore human-dog communication beyond the conveying of human intent and to consider the complexity of communication, beyond directives.

MB: How does your work differ from others concerned with some of the same general topics?

SP: I think the main difference is that I am deliberately cautious about assigning a simple and universal meaning to the gesture.

It can be tempting to create a human-canine dictionary: This gesture means this, that posture means that. But communication is rarely that simple.

The same gesture can occur in very different interactions and produce different responses. Its meaning may be dynamic. A soft gesture and facial expression offered to a nervous dog is not equivalent to an abrupt hand movement meant to act as a directive.

Through my observations and this paper, I aim to problematise the oversimplification of gestures in human-dog communication and open the door to greater complexity, both in how gestures are used and in the meanings they carry.

MB: Are you hopeful that as people learn more about how dogs communicate, they will treat them with greater understanding, compassion, and respect?

SP: Absolutely. I believe that conflict, whether among humans or between species, can arise from breakdowns in communication. Restoring communicative channels is important.

A human who can reassure with gestures is better equipped to show up for a nervous dog. A dog who feels supported during uncertainty is less likely to engage in defensive behaviour, and thus is perceived as calmer, making people less fearful and more open to understanding that dog.

A human who wishes to reassure a dog is also likely to be paying attention to the dog's emotions in situations where the dog needs support. Recognising a dog's emotional needs is, in itself, a pathway toward compassion, empathy, and respect.

item.title: How We Can Deal With Our Fears
item.description:
Fear

How We Can Deal With Our Fears

Should you always confront your fears, or try to ignore them?

Posted August 30, 2026

Key points
  • We may not know the source of our fears.
  • We can confront our fears intentionally and unintentionally.
  • Try as we may, fearful experiences cannot always be avoided.
  • Sometimes we need professional psychological help dealing with our fears.
Source: biancavandijk/Pixabay

Nearly all of us experience fear at some time or other. Fear is a negative emotion, a reaction to perceived real or imagined threats. With fear come psychological and physiological effects. Sources of fear are myriad. An abusive spouse, a potential job loss, a dreaded health diagnosis.

At the recent annual meeting of the American Psychological Association in Washington, D.C., I attended a session about the mental health of Ukrainian civilians and efforts to help them. I thought about the extreme fear, and the loss of life, that comes from night after night of bombs falling on their cities and neighborhoods. Just thinking about it was overpowering. I left the session early.

Sometimes we do not know or understand the source of our fears. Growing up I had a fear of knives and of surgery. I prayed not to have appendicitis. I never had appendicitis but in 2010 I almost died. I had a mesenteric venous thrombosis—the veins around part of my small intestine were clogged. Eighteen inches of my small intestine were dead and had to be removed. After that experience my fear of surgeries and knives went away. It was as if I had gone to sleep and then awakened. Unintentionally I had confronted my fears.

We try to avoid experiences we see as having harmful outcomes. Sometimes, however, a fear-inducing experience cannot be avoided. Early in my life I knew I wanted to fly airplanes. When I was 12, I learned about the United States Air Force Academy. Gaining a congressional appointment to the Air Force Academy became my goal. I knew the Academy would be hard but I thought I could do it. Then I saw a film about the Academy and saw cadets jumping off a 10-meter (almost 33 feet) platform. The fact that if I were a cadet, someday I would have to jump from that tower was fearful. I was fortunate and gained an appointment. The fear was now real and filled me with dread. Someday I would have to jump from that tower. The thought gnawed at me. I knew what I had to do.

That first summer at the Academy was extremely difficult, totally regimented. I finally got some free time on a Sunday afternoon and went to the natatorium. I watched cadets jumping from the tower for fun, an idea hard to grasp. After a half hour or so, I asked one of the cadets how to safely jump from the tower. He told me to jump away from the platform, keep my legs crossed and my body as straight as possible. The walk up to the top was hard, frightening. I walked to the edge, did not look down, and jumped into the air: 1.4 seconds later, at 35 mph, I hit the water. I was sore for a couple days but my fear was gone. I knew I could do it. I had intentionally confronted my fear.

article continues after advertisement

Sometimes we need help dealing with our fears. It may be a matter of reframing how we see that which causes the fear in us. Psychologists and other psychological professionals have a variety of methods, such as cognitive behavioral therapy, through which they can help. In 2016 I needed a somewhat risky surgery. I was not afraid of the surgery but was fearful of leaving my wife on her own should I not survive. With help from the psychologist on my health team, I successfully dealt with that fear. I could not have done so on my own.

The Academy story adapted from my chapter “Be Prepared to Lead” in The Experience of Leadership, edited by Fred Stuvek, Jr. Used with permission.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.
